title: Slow-cooker ragù bianco
subtitle: A white pork ragu, rich with wine and milk, for pasta
excerpt: Pork mince cooked slowly with white wine, milk, and aromatics into a silky, creamy sauce with no tomatoes. Serve with wide pasta such as pappardelle or tagliatelle.
sourceNotes: Ragù bianco is a tomato-free meat sauce traditional in central and northern Italy, including Emilia-Romagna, Tuscany, and Veneto. Unlike the red ragù associated with Bologna, the white version uses wine, milk, and aromatics rather than tomatoes.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the sauce in portions for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge and reheat gently on the hob.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The ragù improves over 24 to 48 hours in the fridge. Make ahead and reheat gently.

glossaryTerms.definition: A white meat sauce from central and northern Italy that uses wine and milk in place of tomatoes. It is slower and richer than a tomato-based sauce and is served with wide pasta shapes.

content.text: is a white pork sauce that makes no use of tomatoes. It gets its silky body from a small amount of whole milk added at the start of cooking. The milk softens the pork and adds a gentle creaminess to the finished sauce. The result is quite different from a tomato ragù, and considerably quieter.

Browning the mince in a pan first makes a real difference here. The slow cooker cannot create the browned, caramelised notes that a hot pan does. If you have 10 minutes, brown the mince before it goes in.
Serve over pappardelle or tagliatelle. Finish with finely grated Parmesan and a grind of black pepper.
Heat a large frying pan over high heat. Add {{pork-mince}} of pork mince and cook for 5 to 7 minutes, breaking it up, until browned. Transfer to the slow cooker.

Add {{onion}} diced onion, {{carrot}} of diced carrot, {{celery}} of diced celery, and {{garlic}} of crushed garlic to the slow cooker. Pour in {{white-wine-dry}} of dry white wine, {{whole-milk}} of whole milk, and {{stock-chicken}} of chicken stock. Add {{thyme}} of thyme and {{bay-leaves}} of bay. Season with {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt and {{black-pepper-ground}} of pepper.

Set the slow cooker to LOW and cook for 5 to 6 hours. The sauce will be thicker than a tomato ragù. Discard the thyme and bay leaves. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve over fresh or dried wide pasta.

rows.symptom: The sauce has a slightly curdled texture
rows.cause: The milk can curdle slightly when added with wine, especially if the heat is too high.
rows.fix: Stir vigorously. The texture will even out. Adding the milk at the end of cooking rather than the start prevents this.

rows.symptom: The sauce is very thin and liquid
rows.cause: The pork released a lot of liquid, and the wine and stock added more.
rows.fix: Set to HIGH with the lid off for 30 minutes to reduce. Stir frequently. The sauce will concentrate and cling to the pasta once reduced.

rows.symptom: The pork tastes grey and lacks flavour
rows.cause: The mince was not browned before cooking.
rows.fix: Nothing can be done now. Next time brown the mince in a hot pan for 5 to 7 minutes before adding to the slow cooker.

rows.cause: The wine did not fully cook off during the slow cook.
rows.fix: Set to HIGH with the lid off for 15 minutes. The remaining alcohol will evaporate.

content.text: Ragù bianco is less well known outside Italy than the red version but is equally rooted in the Italian tradition of long-cooked meat sauces. It is associated with Tuscany and Emilia-Romagna, where pork and white wine are plentiful. The slow cooker version is a practical way to make a sauce that is usually left on the hob for several hours: it goes in the pot in the morning and is ready by dinner.
